claim: Confidence has three separable parts: bias (level), sensitivity (does it separate right from wrong) and efficiency (meta-d'/d'). Calibration (ECE) alone cannot show discrimination: a constant 75% can be perfectly calibrated with zero discrimination.
agent_test: Report AUROC and ECE both for the agent's stated confidence on a fixed item set; add M-ratio if confidence is ordinal.
audit_note: The 75% constant-confidence example is not literally in Fleming and Lau (they distinguish calibration/bias from discrimination/sensitivity and efficiency); it is a mathematically correct illustration.

claim: Raw verbalized LLM confidence is overconfident and discriminates weakly: average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna; GPT-4 AUROC about 62.7% (chance 50%). Re-opened and confirmed in the Xiong PDF.
agent_test: Measure the agent's verbalized confidence AUROC at equal tokens against a plain prompt.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Low ECE can be an artefact of accuracy: GPT-4 on GSM8K gets ECE 0.064 by saying 100% for everything (93.6% accuracy). ECE must be read with AUROC.
agent_test: Always report AUROC next to ECE; reject a calibration gain that comes with flat AUROC.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Sampling consistency can be a strong confidence signal on arithmetic: in Xiong et al., 5 samples with consistency aggregation lifted GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7% (five-dataset average about 56.4% to 73.0%), while Kapoor et al. find sampling-based methods discriminate weakly on open-ended MMLU. It costs extra samples, so it must be compared at equal tokens.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare 1 answer plus verbal confidence vs k answers with agreement as confidence.
audit_note: Xiong et al. do report GSM8K AUROC 54.8 to 92.7 (5 samples with consistency vs Top-K verbalized), but that is the arithmetic best case (five-dataset average 56.4 to 73.0), and Kapoor et al. find sampling methods give good calibration but very weak discrimination on open-ended MMLU.
claim_before_audit: Sampling consistency across several answers is a strong confidence signal: 5 samples lifted GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7%. It costs extra samples, so it must be compared at equal tokens.

claim: Fine-tuned or probed confidence beats prompted confidence (Kapoor et al.): prompted-method ECE does not improve with base model quality, AUROC improves only slightly, and zero-shot prompting stays well behind their worst fine-tuned model (LLaMA-2 7B). A scaffold without training would be limited to prompted or sampled confidence (inference, not a measured result).
agent_test: Not testable without training; the scaffold can only use prompting plus sampling plus temperature scaling on a dev set.
audit_note: Kapoor et al. say prompted-method ECE does not improve with base model quality but AUROC does improve slightly, the gap to fine-tuning stays large versus their worst fine-tuned model, and verbal elicitation is on par with weaker fine-tuning methods in discrimination; 'not usable by a scaffold with no training' is the researcher's inference, not a finding.
claim_before_audit: Fine-tuned or probed confidence beats prompted confidence: prompted methods do not improve with base model quality; even the best prompted model trails the worst fine-tuned one. Not usable by a scaffold with no training.

claim: Verbalized confidence can beat token probabilities for RLHF chat models: TriviaQA ECE 0.140 label-prob vs 0.068 verbalized top-1 vs 0.050 top-2 (Tian). Xiong finds white-box and black-box AUROC close (0.522 to 0.605).
agent_test: Elicit top-2 or top-k verbalized answers with probabilities, compare with single-answer confidence.
audit_note: Tian numbers match one table (TriviaQA 0.140 / 0.068 / 0.050); Xiong says white-box methods are better with a narrow gap, so 'close' is fair; the two papers pull in slightly different directions.

claim: Users do not read LLM confidence well. Human AUC on LLM answers was only about .59 to .60 vs model AUC .75 to .78; explanation length raised user confidence (BF=25) without raising their accuracy. Uncertainty wording narrowed the gap.
agent_test: Test whether a calibrated wording ('I am unsure, about 60%') in the final answer shifts a simulated reader's AUC.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Metacognitive information (signal-detection measure) differs about 2-fold between models (1.98-fold, 4 open models, 224,000 trials) and is domain-specific: weakest in Science and Technology for all four models. After re-scoring in v3 the link to accuracy is -0.80 on TriviaQA and 0.00 on Natural Questions (v1/v2 said -1.00 and a two-fold range driven by a length-biased scorer). Servajean (2026) finds M-ratio steadier across tasks than AUROC for two of three current models.
agent_test: Compute AUROC and an efficiency measure per domain for the agent; check that accuracy and metacognition move apart and that the weakest domain is flagged.

claim: Coarse scale choice hurts measurement: the three most frequent values hold 78.2 to 92.1% of 0-100 answers; baseline M-ratio ranges 0.62 to 0.92. AUROC can rise while ECE worsens when confidence is coarsened: in Yoon et al., removing epistemic markers pushed the model onto two bins (95% and 65%), so ECE went 0.042 to 0.109 while AUROC went 0.782 to 0.837 on TriviaQA.
agent_test: Elicit confidence on a 0-10 or verbal 5-level scale and test which gives best AUROC.
audit_note: Dai and Wang numbers match (Top-3 78.2-92.1%, M-ratio 0.62-0.92), but Yoon et al. show the AUROC rise comes from REMOVING epistemic markers (the model then uses only two bins, 95% and 65%, so ECE worsens 0.042 to 0.109 while AUROC rises 0.782 to 0.837), not from epistemic markers coarsening confidence.
claim_before_audit: Coarse scale choice hurts measurement: three values hold 78.2 to 92.1% of 0-100 answers; baseline M-ratio ranges 0.62 to 0.92. AUROC can rise when ECE worsens because epistemic markers coarsen confidence (0.782 to 0.837 AUROC while ECE 0.042 to 0.109).

claim: Reasoning before stating confidence helps in one study (no CoT: ECE 0.150 / AUROC 0.689 vs original 0.042 / 0.782 on TriviaQA), but newer evidence on current reasoning models is mixed. Del 2026: confidence stated with the answer is about as good as a later judge pass (AUROC 69-74 math); longer thinking budgets worsen calibration on a climate-confidence task (Lacombe 2025); reasoning-model confidence bunches on a few high values (70-90% of responses on under 7 values) and ignores hesitation in the trace (Yang 2026, VLMs). No study isolates confidence-before vs after reasoning at equal tokens.
agent_test: Compare confidence asked before reasoning, after reasoning, and after a backtracking pass at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs show choice-supportive bias: change-of-mind 32.5% with answer hidden vs 13.1% with it shown; opposing advice overweighted (85.0% hidden vs 39.2% shown). The bias disappears when the visible earlier answer is attributed to another LLM (31.3% hidden vs 33.2% shown, n.s.). The effect on final accuracy of a revise step was not measured in any study found. Related: debate overconfidence study (72.9% initial confidence vs rational 50%, rising to 83.3%).
agent_test: Give the agent its own earlier answer visible vs masked in the review step; measure switch rate and accuracy.
audit_note: Kumaran et al. reported in the same paper (four evidence lines are one source); only Prasad and Nguyen is a second independent paper, and it supports just the debate-confidence clause.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without outside signal does not help and often hurts: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (3 calls) and 41.8 (5 calls); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0. Re-opened and confirmed; table columns are number of calls, not rounds.
agent_test: Run revise operator with and without an external check; confidence-gated revise only when confidence is low.

claim: Confidence-gated stopping saves cost with a usable score: BrowseConf-Zero 41.3 vs 36.7 accuracy with 5.67 vs 10 attempts on BrowseComp (no gain on BrowseComp-zh); CAS up to 12.33x budget saving vs majority voting and 5.19 vs 12.87 samples against Adaptive-Consistency; CGES 16.0 -> 6.7 calls (58% fewer) within 0.4 points. The gate needs calibrated or token-level confidence (CAS and CGES use RL-trained confidence or token probabilities). No test on ARC or BrainTeaser. Even the 90-94% confidence bin was only 53.33% accurate on BrowseComp.
agent_test: Gate a second attempt on stated confidence on ARC and BrainTeaser items; compare to fixed-n resampling at equal total tokens.

claim: Tools shift calibration in one study (Xuan 2026): evidence tools such as web search cause overconfidence; verification tools such as a code interpreter reduce miscalibration. Calibration-aware RL cut ECE up to 68% but needs training, and in some rows AUROC fell while ECE improved. A second study points the other way: search-augmented answering gave 89.3% vs 48.7% for pure reasoning on a climate-confidence task (Lacombe 2025). No independent replication of the tool dichotomy was found.
agent_test: Compare confidence after search vs after code execution on the same questions.

claim: Human metacognition: 5 of 6 cross-task meta-d'/d' correlations were significant (N=181, four 2AFC tasks). Fleming 2010 (opened): N=32, accuracy held near 71%, Aroc 0.55-0.75, uncorrelated with accuracy (r=-0.11), split-half r=0.69, right anterior PFC grey matter link. But Rahnev 2024 (1,091 subjects) finds M-ratio test-retest only r=.17-.42 (50-400 trials). For LLMs, efficiency is domain-specific (Cacioli 2026) and only partly stable across tasks (Servajean 2026), so a general LLM metacognition factor is not supported.
agent_test: Check whether an agent's AUROC rank over domains is stable across tasks.

claim: The Dunning-Kruger pattern may be a statistical artefact: a noise-plus-censoring model reproduces the gap after adjusting for group mean. The original paper was not opened here.
agent_test: Do not use skill-linked overconfidence as a design premise; measure on the agent directly.

claim: Confidence is a second-order inference (Fleming and Daw): confidence can come apart from accuracy through extra read-out noise, post-decision evidence and inaccessible evidence. This predicts that evidence gathered after answering should be used to update confidence.
agent_test: Allow a post-answer evidence step; test whether confidence after it separates right from wrong better.

claim: Distractor and 'none of the above' manipulations change LLM accuracy and calibration: none-of-the-above lowers both; explicit distractors can lower miscalibration (up to 90% ECE cut best case, abstract only).
agent_test: Re-run confidence elicitation with and without added distractor options.

claim: In current reasoning models, one stated confidence per run is a strong signal, and the best use of a second sample is to mix its agreement into the score. Math AUROC: VC@1 71.3, SC@2 about 70, hybrid SCVC@2 84.2 (best single signal at K=8: 81.4). Gains after K=2 are +2.7 (to K=5) and about +1.5 (to K=8). Domain-dependent: smaller in STEM and humanities. Only 3 open mid-size models.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare: 1 run + stated confidence; 2 runs + agreement mixed with confidence; 5 runs majority.

claim: Self-consistency is weaker than verbalized confidence at equal small sample counts in reasoning models (SC@2: 70.5 math, 66.6 STEM, 63.3 humanities; SC@8 still below VC@8). This reverses the older non-reasoning-model picture where consistency lifted AUROC strongly (Xiong: 54.8 to 92.7 GSM8K). Crossover not found within K<=8.
agent_test: Do not use k<=5 agreement alone as confidence for a reasoning-model agent.

claim: Calibration training can lower ECE without raising AUROC, and the gain may not transfer: in Wang et al., supervised CalibSFT alone cut OOD ECE from 46.94 to 25.49 while OOD AUROC fell from 65.71 to 61.20 (confidence-aware RL later restored it above 71%); in Xuan et al., CAR lowers ECE and raises AUROC in the main tests but lowers AUROC in the real-API transfer test (Qwen2.5-7B 0.831 to 0.790, Qwen3-4B 0.825 to 0.765). Off-the-shelf reasoning models put their verbalized confidence on a few high values (fewer than 5% of responses below 0.5, 70-90% on fewer than 7 values).
agent_test: Reject any calibration fix that does not show AUROC held or improved on a held-out domain.
audit_note: Numbers are real but come from specific methods: ECE 46.94 to 25.49 with AUROC 65.71 to 61.20 is Wang et al.'s supervised CalibSFT alone (their confidence-aware RL then lifts OOD AUROC to over 71%), and Xuan et al.'s CAR raises AUROC in the main Table 2 (up to 17% relative); it lowers AUROC only in the Serper-API transfer test (Qwen2.5-7B 0.831 to 0.790, Qwen3-4B 0.825 to 0.765).
claim_before_audit: Calibration training lowers ECE without reliably raising AUROC, and the gain may not transfer: ECE 46.94 -> 25.49 out of distribution with AUROC 65.71 -> 61.20; CAR rows with ECE down and AUROC down. Off-the-shelf reasoning models have confidence prior concentrated on a few high values.

claim: Post-hoc recalibration (temperature or Platt scaling) does not reliably carry out of domain: partial gains for Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B, none significant for Llama 3.1 8B; Platt is better when the held-out set is small. A single temperature fit on 250 items (Luo and Jho) is not shown to persist.
agent_test: Refit the calibration map per domain and test on another domain before trusting it.

claim: Human metacognition measures are reliable within a session but not across days: split-half r above .837 at 100 trials, but M-ratio test-retest r = .168 (50 trials), .235 (100), .293 (200), .422 (400). Non-normalised measures (meta-d', AUC2) depend strongly on difficulty (Cohen's d 1.5-2.6); M-ratio mostly does not (significant in 1 of 4 datasets).
agent_test: Use hundreds of items for any M-ratio on the agent; report AUROC and M-ratio, keep difficulty fixed.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Hedged wording changes human readers: first-person 'I'm not sure, but...' lowered agreement with the AI (80.9% control to 74.8%) and confidence (3.95 to 3.66), and raised participant accuracy; impersonal hedges were weaker and not significant (N=404). No study found tests this wording on a model reader or reports reader AUC.
agent_test: For human-facing answers use first-person hedges; for a later agent step use a number, and test reader AUC.

claim: No evidence was found for confidence gating or masking on ARC or BrainTeaser specifically, for scale granularity on current models beyond the 3-value collapse in Dai and Wang, or for confidence-before vs after reasoning at equal tokens. These stay as project tests.
agent_test: Run the three tests in the critique GAPS list on the project's own benchmarks.
